title: Counting spanning trees: edge-subset enumeration vs Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem (Bareiss)
problem_statement: Given a simple undirected graph G on n >= 1 vertices as its symmetric 0/1 adjacency matrix (zero diagonal), output the number tau(G) of spanning trees of G as an exact integer. tau(G) = 0 if G is disconnected, and the 1-vertex graph has exactly one spanning tree (the empty edge set), so tau = 1 for n = 1. n = 0 is not part of the problem.

input.parameter: n = number of vertices (n >= 1); m = number of edges, m <= n(n-1)/2.
input.size_measure: An n x n adjacency matrix: n^2 bits (n(n-1)/2 independent entries). The output satisfies tau(G) <= n^(n-2) (G is a subgraph of K_n; Cayley's formula), so it has at most (n-2) log2(n) + 1 bits.

algorithms.name: enumeration of all (n-1)-edge subsets
algorithms.idea: List the m edges and try each of the C(m, n-1) subsets of n-1 edges, counting those that are acyclic. Acyclicity is tested with a fresh union-find per subset (union by size, path halving), rejecting the subset at the first edge whose endpoints are already joined. An acyclic set of n-1 edges on n vertices is a spanning tree.
algorithms.pseudocode: E = edges of G; count = 0; for each (n-1)-subset T of E (itertools.combinations): make n singleton sets; for (u, v) in T: if find(u) == find(v): reject T; union(u, v); if T was not rejected: count += 1; return count
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) to read the matrix, plus C(m, n-1) subsets at Theta(n) each to reset the union-find arrays and at most n-1 unions (2(n-1) finds; O(n alpha(n)) amortized with union by size and path halving): O(n alpha(n) C(m, n-1)) and Omega(n C(m, n-1)). C(m, n-1) grows with m, so the worst case is K_n, m = n(n-1)/2: (n/2)^(n-1) <= C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) <= (e n/2)^(n-1), i.e. 2^Theta(n log n), super-exponential in n.
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(m + n) beyond the input (the edge list, one subset, two union-find arrays)
algorithms.correctness: Every spanning tree has exactly n-1 edges, and a set of k edges on n vertices without a cycle is a forest with n-k components, so an (n-1)-edge set is a spanning tree iff it is acyclic. Union-find finds a cycle exactly when an edge joins two vertices that are already in one component. itertools.combinations yields every (n-1)-subset once, so every spanning tree is counted once. For n = 1 the single (empty) subset is counted: tau = 1. If m < n-1 there are no subsets and the answer is 0.

algorithms.name: Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem with Bareiss fraction-free elimination
algorithms.idea: tau(G) is the determinant of the Laplacian L = D - A with one row and the same column deleted. Compute that (n-1) x (n-1) integer determinant exactly with Bareiss's fraction-free elimination, in which every intermediate value is an integer minor and every division is exact.
algorithms.pseudocode: M = L with the last row and column deleted; N = n-1; if N == 0: return 1; sign = 1; prev = 1; for k = 0..N-2: if M[k][k] == 0: swap row k with a lower row r with M[r][k] != 0 and set sign = -sign, or return 0 if there is none; for i, j = k+1..N-1: M[i][j] = (M[i][j] * M[k][k] - M[i][k] * M[k][j]) / prev (exact); prev = M[k][k]; return sign * M[N-1][N-1]
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) arithmetic operations: exactly (n-2)(n-1)(2n-3)/2 multiplications and exact divisions on every connected graph (no zero pivot occurs), at most that many otherwise (it stops at the first zero pivot), plus Theta(n^2) additions to build the Laplacian. The integers are not of constant size: every intermediate entry is a minor of the reduced Laplacian, of absolute value < n^(n-1) by Hadamard's inequality (each row has Euclidean norm <= sqrt(n(n-1)) < n), and a product before division is < 2 n^(2(n-1)), so all values have O(n log n) bits. Bit complexity O(n^3 M(n log n)), where M(b) is the cost of multiplying b-bit integers (O(n^5 log^2 n) with schoolbook multiplication): polynomial in the n^2-bit input.
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n^2) integers of O(n log n) bits each
algorithms.correctness: Kirchhoff 1847 (matrix-tree theorem): every cofactor of the Laplacian equals the number of spanning trees, and it is 0 for a disconnected graph. Bareiss 1968: by Sylvester's identity, after step k each entry M[i][j] (i, j > k) equals the minor of the input on rows {0..k, i} and columns {0..k, j}, so the division by the previous pivot is exact and the last diagonal entry is the determinant. Swapping two rows below the leading block permutes the input's rows (one sign change) and keeps this invariant. If a pivot and every entry below it are zero, the trailing block has a zero column, and Sylvester's identity (det of the trailing block = prev^(size-1) * det) gives det = 0. On reduced Laplacians the swap branch is never taken: the reduced Laplacian is positive definite iff G is connected, so all pivots (leading principal minors) are positive, and if G is disconnected the first zero pivot has a zero column below it (the Bareiss block is a positive multiple of a Schur complement of a positive semidefinite matrix). The branch is exercised on general integer matrices in the experiment script.

relationship: Super-exponential -> polynomial: on K_n the enumeration tries C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) = 2^Theta(n log n) edge subsets, while the matrix-tree theorem turns counting into one (n-1) x (n-1) determinant, Theta(n^3) arithmetic operations on O(n log n)-bit integers. Listing only the spanning trees would not rescue the enumeration: K_n has n^(n-2) of them (Cayley's formula), so any method that touches each tree is super-exponential on dense graphs. The determinant is what makes counting easy where listing is not.

sources.title: A theorem on trees
sources.venue: Quarterly Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics 23, 376-378
sources.note: No DOI. K_n has n^(n-2) spanning trees; used in harness.check and as the upper bound tau(G) <= n^(n-2).

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree for n = 1..8 (enumeration capped at n = 8; K_8 has 1,184,040 edge subsets) on a mix of random G(n, p) with p in {0.2, 0.5, 0.8}, complete graphs, random trees, trees plus extra edges, cycles and graphs built disconnected, all randomly relabelled; Kirchhoff alone also at n = 12, 20, 40. harness.check shares no code with the implementations: it returns 0 for disconnected graphs (depth-first search), 1 for connected graphs with n-1 edges (trees), n^(n-2) for complete graphs (Cayley), deletion-contraction on multigraphs (with memoisation) for up to 24 edges, and otherwise the determinant of a different cofactor (row and column 0 deleted) by Gaussian elimination over the rationals; it also requires 0 <= answer <= n^(n-2). V2, Kirchhoff (measure: reported): the harness's CountingInt entries count every multiplication and division of the unchanged implementation; on K_n, n = 16, 32, 64, 128, the counts are 3045, 28365, 244125, 2024253 = (n-2)(n-1)(2n-3)/2 exactly (proven from the loop structure, checked in the experiment script for every n = 1..70 and n = 128; random connected graphs give the same count). The experiment script also runs the Bareiss routine on 600 general integer matrices against the Leibniz formula (all equal; 326 needed a row swap) and on the reduced Laplacians of 2000 random graphs (509 disconnected), where no row swap ever occurred, as predicted. Fitted against (n-1)^3 (the cube of the reduced dimension) with tolerance 0.03: alpha = 1.014 (the lower-order terms); rivals n^4 (alpha 0.781) and n^2 (alpha 1.562) are rejected, and the log-factor diagnostic is resolved (alpha 0.933 against (n-1)^3 log n, 1.111 against (n-1)^3 / log n). V2, enumeration (measure: time): it does no arithmetic on the entries (it only tests them for truth), so an instrumented number type cannot see its per-subset work without changing the implementation; it is timed by the validator (best of 3 repeats, each a loop of at least 20 ms) on K_n, n = 4..8, against n C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) with the default tolerance 0.25; rivals n! and 2^n must not fit. Two runs on 2026-10-06 (other agents running): alpha = 0.961 and 0.995; rival alphas n! 1.512 / 1.566 and 2^n 4.051 / 4.199, all rejected. Timing cannot separate the claim from n^(n-2) (noise-free alpha 1.20 over n = 4..8) or from C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) without the factor n (1.06); see caveats.

caveats: The Theta(n^3) bound counts arithmetic operations; the integers grow to O(n log n) bits (tau(K_n) = n^(n-2) itself has about n log2 n bits), so the bit cost is higher, but polynomial (see the algorithm's time_complexity). Computing the determinant modulo several primes and combining by the Chinese remainder theorem is the usual alternative; it is not implemented. The enumeration's V2 is a timing fit (tolerance 0.25), so it confirms super-exponential growth of the claimed shape and rejects n! and 2^n, but it cannot distinguish n C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) from nearby super-exponential costs such as n^(n-2) or C(n(n-1)/2, n-1); its alpha(n) factor is invisible at these sizes. The enumeration's running time depends on m: on sparse graphs C(m, n-1) is much smaller (1 for a tree), so V2 uses K_n, its worst case. n = 0 is excluded because conventions differ (the 0 x 0 determinant is 1, but the empty graph is often called disconnected).
notes: Neighbours in the dataset: minimum-spanning-tree-brute-vs-kruskal enumerates the same (n-1)-edge subsets to optimise instead of count; determinant-cofactor-vs-gaussian is the determinant step on its own (over GF(p)); permanent-naive-vs-ryser shows that the sign-free analogue of the determinant is #P-complete.
